title: Window head and sill in a framed or cavity wall

checklist.item: Sill has a sloped sub-sill pan flashing with a back dam and end dams, draining to the exterior.
checklist.why: Windows leak at the corners of the sill; the pan is what catches it.

checklist.item: Head flashing (drip cap) laps under the water barrier above and extends past the jambs, with end dams.
checklist.why: Reverse-lapped head flashing sends water into the opening.

checklist.item: Water barrier and flashing membrane are lapped shingle fashion around the opening: sill first, jambs, then head.
checklist.why: The lap order is the whole water management strategy.

checklist.item: Air barrier is sealed to the window frame on all four sides, with backer rod and sealant or a transition membrane shown.
checklist.why: The frame perimeter is the largest air leak in most walls.

checklist.item: The thermal break of the frame lines up with the wall insulation; lintel or sill angle does not bridge the insulation without a thermal break.
checklist.why: Misaligned insulation makes a cold frame that condenses.

checklist.item: Shim space, anchor type and spacing, sealant joint size, and a weep path at the sill are labelled.
checklist.why: Unlabelled joints are sized on site, usually too small.

checklist.item: Glazing and frame meet the wildfire exposure requirements (for example tempered or multi-pane glazing) where the site is in a fire hazard severity zone.
checklist.why: Windows are the first element to fail in a wildfire.
